column3: It nearly repeats surrendering one's face to God with beneficence, while adding its reward and freedom from fear and grief.
It locates the spirit within God's affair and limits human knowledge, only broadly supporting humility before the final return of affairs.
It contrasts a warranted holding to a revealed book with inherited imitation, clarifying what makes a firm attachment sound.
It repeats the focus formulation and adds Abraham's upright way and God's friendship as its lived horizon.
It exposes those who acknowledge God as Creator yet lack knowledge, sharpening the local contrast with genuine submission.
Its condemnation of responses to a daughter's birth does not materially explain submission, beneficence, or the firm handhold.
It explicitly names the unbreakable firm handhold and frames it as faith in God after rejecting false powers.
Its etiquette within a shared undertaking offers only a remote practical instance of faithful responsibility.
It explicitly presents surrendering one's face to God as guidance and distinguishes proclamation from controlling the outcome.
It supplies the contrary case of precarious worship that turns away under trial, showing why the focus's attachment must be firm.
God's ownership of all in heaven and earth provides local background for entrusting all affairs to Him.
It joins righteous public action with the same conclusion that the outcome of affairs belongs to God.
It directly restates that all affairs return to God, in a setting of perseverance amid rejection.
The report of settled morning punishment adds no distinct explanation of the focus.
It makes the good outcome belong to the God-conscious and connects that prospect with patient endurance.
It repeats the return of all affairs to God and grounds it in His dominion over heaven and earth.
Its statement about creation and resurrection as one soul does not clarify the focus's call to submission and beneficence.
It shows an affair bearing its own ruinous consequence, making the focus's final outcome morally consequential.
It directly repeats that affairs return to God while placing even messengers within that ultimate return.
Its claim that every affair settles offers a broad parallel to the focus's finality of affairs.
The divine names of peace, security, and guardianship only indirectly resonate with the focus's secure attachment.
It directly repeats that all affairs return to God, reinforced by His possession of all creation.
It identifies the beneficent as recipients of guidance and mercy in the focus surah's opening frame.
It states the fitting recompense of beneficence, extending the focus's qualification of the submitter as a doer of good.
Its description of a darkened face at news of a daughter is unrelated to directing one's face to God.
The identification of Aaron as Moses's brother does not illuminate the focus.
The prior covenant and summons to faith add a commitment dimension to holding firmly to God.
It joins personal purification with the return to God, supplying an individual-responsibility setting for the focus's end.
Its local command to avoid pride gives concrete ethical form to the beneficence named in the focus.
The prophets' covenant offers a general image of binding commitment but is less direct than earlier handhold passages.
Its report of a darkened face in an idolatrous comparison does not explain facing God in submission.
The request to strengthen Moses through Aaron is not a useful link to the focus.
Holding fast to the Book together with prayer and reform gives an active communal expression of steadfast attachment.
Its call to consider the warned people's outcome only generally parallels the final outcome of affairs.
God's bringing forth even a hidden mustard seed supplies the local accountability basis for entrusting outcomes to Him.
The solemn covenant of the prophets adds an image of a weighty, durable commitment.
It traces evil action into an evil end, supplying the negative moral trajectory opposite the focus's secure course.
The rescue and drowning in Noah's story add no distinct account of the focus's key terms.
It makes a shared sequence of deception culminate in a shared lasting end, illustrating consequential outcomes.
Its contrast between a beneficent descendant and a manifest wrongdoer adds only a brief moral distinction.
It names the surah's faithful recipients as being on guidance and successful, supporting the focus's positive trajectory.
Seeking the face of the highest Lord gives a related orientation of intention, but does not add submission or the handhold.
Its punitive binding is a contrast to the chosen, secure attachment in the focus.
It contrasts people fragmenting their affair with the certainty that all return to God.
It sharply limits human control over repentance and punishment, clarifying the focus's reservation of final affairs to God.
It explicitly links holding fast to God with guidance to a straight path, a close counterpart to the firm handhold.
Its sincere devotion during danger and subsequent inconsistency offer the local contrast to settled submission.
Fulfilling God's covenant without breaking it gives a durable-commitment analogue to the firm handhold.
Its detailed rules for accidental killing do not add a focused explanation of the verse.
The names First and Last provide only general theological background for all affairs returning to God.
It directly pairs God's nearness with the God-conscious and the beneficent, strengthening the focus's ethical condition.
The ruinous outcome of corrupters is a general negative counterpart already covered by stronger outcome passages.
Its local command of gratitude and return to God provides limited surrounding context.
The late wish to become beneficent underscores the consequence of missed action, though the theme is already established.
Its command to retain or release with good conduct gives a concrete but specialized use of holding with beneficence.
The arrival of God's command after self-deception offers only a broad account of eventual outcome.
Patient forgiveness as resolute conduct gives a limited ethical example of acting well.
The greeting of peace to Abraham evokes the favorable end of his submission, though that submission is not stated here.
The local command for measured walking and lowered voice concretizes the humble conduct fitting beneficence.
The seal and fragrance of the drink do not materially explain the focus's secure attachment or return.
Its retain-or-release rule with beneficence is a specialized, less direct ethical parallel.
Its diversion from God's path gives a local negative contrast but little further explanation of the focus.
It insists that the whole affair belongs to God, correcting attempts to possess or predict the outcome.
The covenant's worship, support, and good loan connect faithful commitment with promised forgiveness and gardens.
It moves from acknowledging God's management of affairs to the practical demand for God-consciousness.
It associates doing good with good in this world and the better abode of the God-conscious.
Its declaration of freedom from idolatry does not substantially develop the focus after earlier submission passages.
God's ordered alternation of night and day and knowledge of deeds provide broad local context for His final judgment.
Its coerced submission on the Day contrasts sharply with the focus's voluntary submission to God.
The command to accept peace in a conflict is only a distant use of a related root.
Its brief worldly enjoyment followed by severe punishment supplies a local but already familiar outcome contrast.
The instantaneous divine command only broadly supports God's decisive control of affairs.
It makes each person share in the consequence of good or bad intercession, extending accountable action.
The severe seizure of unjust towns adds a redundant illustration of adverse outcome.
God's holding birds aloft gives a concrete image of sustaining support, though it is not the focus's moral handhold.
It joins faith and righteous deeds with exalted ranks, reinforcing the focus's union of submission and good action.
As the immediately preceding verse, it contrasts ancestral following with following God's revelation before the focus states true submission.
Its image of birds held in the sky repeats the sustaining-support analogy without adding much beyond the earlier bird verse.
It presents being called to Islam as the alternative to fabricating against God, supporting the focus's orientation of surrender.
Sharing Moses's task with Aaron does not illuminate the focus.
Its description of a decreed affair provides only a general parallel to divine determination of outcomes.
It explicitly commands holding fast to revelation and links that attachment to the straight path.
The preceding local verse contrasts God's visible and hidden favors with argument lacking knowledge, guidance, or illuminating scripture.
Its description of good and beautiful companions does not meaningfully develop beneficent action.
It pairs accepting peace with reliance on God, offering a practical instance of entrusting the outcome to Him.
The request for a family minister is not a useful counterpart to the focus.
The repeated greeting of peace is only indirectly related to the focus's security.
Deliverance from punishment and manifest success offer a general favorable-end parallel.
God's exclusive knowledge of future events gives local background for yielding final affairs to Him.
Commanding God-consciousness is a broad ethical parallel, adding little after stronger passages.
All coming humbled on the Day gives a final-return setting but not the focus's voluntary beneficent submission.
Entering in peace on the day of permanence gives a distant picture of a secure final outcome.
Its appointed end and final abode offer a broad consequence theme without the focus's key relation.
Withheld provision offers a second, less direct instance of divine holding after the stronger support image.
The brief mention of God's favor, mercy, repentance, and wisdom does not explain the focus.
It directly assigns the final outcome to the God-conscious and contrasts it with seeking dominance and corruption.
Its warning that apostasy voids deeds offers a broad negative outcome but little new on the focus.
Following the best of what is heard provides an active discerning response consistent with beneficent guidance.
Its detailed commercial documentation and God-consciousness are only a remote practical ethical parallel.
The abiding face of the Lord gives an eschatological depth to directing one's face to God.
It commands holding fast all together to God's rope, a central communal counterpart to the focus's unbreakable handhold.
It unites the return of every affair to God with worship and reliance on Him, directly expanding the focus's conclusion.
It explicitly commands turning to the Lord and submitting to Him before punishment, making the focus's surrender urgent and consequential.
It states that all affairs reach their final destination with God, closely restating the focus's final clause.
It declares that affairs are returned to God, placing the focus's secure attachment within divine final judgment.
It describes all in heaven and earth submitting willingly or unwillingly and returning to God, contrasting universal return with the focus's voluntary surrender.
It says affairs are returned to God within a concrete trial, showing that human encounter remains under divine determination.
Reliance on God as sufficient gives a practical posture corresponding to holding the secure handhold.
It joins resolved action with reliance on God, explaining how human effort coexists with entrusting the outcome to Him.
It reports the command to submit to the Lord of all worlds, giving a direct formulation of the focus's core act.
It calls believers to remain God-conscious and die only in submission, adding perseverance to the focus's settled orientation.
It commands doing good and states God's love for the beneficent, directly supporting the focus's condition of ihsan.
God's command of justice and beneficence gives concrete ethical content to being a doer of good.
It promises divine accompaniment to those who strive in His cause and are beneficent, extending active devotion beyond inward surrender.
It links God-conscious patience with the unrelinquished reward of the beneficent, reinforcing the focus's favorable end.
It places God's mercy near the beneficent, adding a mercy dimension to the focus's moral qualification.
It defines beneficence through giving, restraining anger, and pardoning people, supplying concrete practices for the focus's ihsan.
It assures that God does not waste the reward of beneficent action, further specifying the consequence of steadfast service.
